strengths: The virtual-correspondence construction is an original, practically useful contribution to geometric vision. It turns difficult four-point, three-view estimation problems into calls to established 5pt/6pt and P3P solvers. The mean-based variant requires neither additional image information nor training. Its simplicity and demonstrated utility support weak acceptance.

The geometric formulation correctly distinguishes the calibrated, slightly overconstrained configuration from the minimal shared-focal-length configuration. Supplementary Lemma 1 provides a geometric justification for the mean-point heuristic. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that its solutions are approximate.

The calibrated experiments demonstrate improvements over the tested homotopy-continuation baseline. In Table 1, the mean-plus-shift variant improves AUC@10 from 50.61 to 52.27 on Sacre Coeur and from 32.03 to 32.53 on St. Peters’ Square. Figure 3 supports the benefit of sampling fewer correspondences when inlier ratios are low.

The evaluation includes 10,000 real image triplets, controlled noise and outlier experiments, solver and RANSAC timings, parameter ablations, and informative oracle comparisons. Including the strong 5pt+P3P baseline and acknowledging its superior accuracy in some settings makes the analysis useful beyond the proposed method.

The shared-focal-length extension provides encouraging practical results: Table 2 reports AUC@5 of 72.05 for the mean-plus-shift variant versus 71.73 for 6pt+P3P, with average RANSAC time decreasing from 0.11 to 0.07 seconds. The supplementary two-view experiment also suggests broader applicability.
weaknesses: The claimed advantage under limited computational time is only partially established. Figure 3 compares RANSAC iterations, although iteration costs differ substantially: Table 1 reports 218.71 microseconds for the mean-plus-shift solver versus 77.90 for 5pt+P3P, with learned variants costing still more. The aggregate timings do not establish the accuracy-versus-elapsed-time tradeoff specifically in the high-outlier regimes motivating the method.

The shared-focal-length contribution lacks direct calibration validation. Table 2 and the supplementary noise experiments report pose errors without focal-length errors. KITTI triplets formed from a stereo pair and an adjacent frame provide limited motion diversity, leaving performance across different focal lengths and camera configurations uncertain. Additionally, the three-view pose metric evaluates translation directions but omits relative translation scale, so complete metric reconstruction accuracy is not established.

The approximation has a substantial accuracy floor on noiseless inputs, as Figures 6–7 show. Lemma 1 bounds image-space correspondence error by triangle size; it does not control the resulting pose error. The experiments do not systematically characterize sensitivity to viewing angle, depth variation, or poorly conditioned camera configurations. This limits the guidance available for deciding when the heuristic is reliable.

The learned component offers modest and inconsistent benefits relative to its cost. On Sacre Coeur, Table 1 gives AUC@10 of 52.48 for the learned-plus-shift variant versus 52.27 for the mean-plus-shift variant, while solver time increases from 218.71 to 511.28 microseconds. The calibrated network is also reused for unknown focal length without dedicated training. These results make the learning contribution less convincing than the simple geometric construction.

There are correctable but consequential specification gaps. Equation (2), as written, is a signed normalized epipolar residual rather than a nonnegative Sampson loss; directly minimizing it would not enforce epipolar consistency. The actual training objective therefore needs clarification. Although network architecture and training settings are provided, RANSAC thresholds, stopping settings, and local-refinement details remain insufficiently specified, and source-code availability is only promised in the manuscript.
